newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Coffee reignites as sellers extend quotas.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Coffee reignites as sellers extend quotas.

text.p: A rally in world coffee reignited on Wednesday when producing nations agreed to extend their current cartel-style export quotas for 12 more months to try to lock in gains from this year's spectacular run-up in prices.
At the Coffee Sugar and Cocoa Exchange in New York, arabica coffee futures for July rose 10 cents to top $2.50 per pound after news of the exporters' London accord.
The Association of Coffee Producing Countries (ACPC) led by Brazil ended talks with an accord to limit total exports by the 14 members to 52.75 million (60 kg) bags for the 12 months from July 1.
This is about the same as the volume limit that they had applied under current curbs expiring June 30. A statement said the goal was "to ensure prices remain at a level remunerative to producers".

The deal was cut against a backdrop of a rally that has taken benchmark futures prices for green (unroasted) beans up 80-100 percent since January, because of low stocks and tight Latin American supply.
Consumers are paying up to 50 percent more in the shops as roasters have passed on their higher costs.

Wednesday's firmer New York price at $2.50 per pound for July delivery arabica beans was, however, somewhat below a 20-year high at $2.80 to which the now-expired May contract had risen a few days ago.

And the ACPC is worried that speculative funds could suddenly cash in their gains on the rally and send the market down again, particularly at the end of the Brazilian winter in about 15 weeks' time and if there is no frost to damage the crop there.
So the exporters soon rejected suggestions that quotas be suspended because of the current strength of the market.
They made clear, however, that they did not want high prices to quench consumer demand for coffee, so they made provision to juggle supply within their one-year limit in line with fluctuating demand.
The ACPC said a technical group would monitor conditions and that a seasonal allocation of quotas would not be made until September, to allow a flexible and adequate flow of coffee.
It said the goal was a price that ensured fair return to their own economies "but allowing continuing growth in worldwide consumption of coffee".

Although prices kicked higher on the ACPC news, several traders said that the decisions were somewhat academic just now, with the market scrambling for every bean it can get and exporters disposed to ignore quotas and sell whatever they can.
"I don't think this should have an affect on the market," said Smith Barney analyst Walt Spilka. "I don't think it's an overly effective programme anyway."

But brokerage GNI Ltd said in a commentary that the real test of the ACPC would be how it behaves "when prices fall if the Brazilian crop survives frost damage this winter". - - London Newsroom +44 171 542 7729
